div.div: The second bit flip in an ECC2 error injection happens in the parity bit and not in the standard RAM bytes

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 198px; height: 1px; padding-top: 260px; margin-left: 42px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0px; text-align: left;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: rgb(0, 0, 0); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; overflow-wrap: normal;

div.div:
The AVR64SDxx has a 32-bit (4-byte) RAM buffer. C99 does not guarantee that a variable's address will align to this 4-byte double word. Therefore, an 8-byte array is declared to ensure that no application data is affected by the injection.
This diagram shows the 4 possible alignments of this array relative to the RAM buffer boundaries.
The row with the addressed byte represents the 4 bytes loaded to the RAM buffer.
These 4 tables show that by setting aside 8 bytes we ensure that we never load a byte outside the array for error injection and that the address for the addressed byte 4 always is outside the loaded double word but still inside the array.
